content: All the studies included in the analysis were observational in nature, with five being before-and-after studies and one being a program evaluation study. The methodological quality of all these studies was weak. There was significant indirectness in terms of participants, interventions, and outcomes. The components of the interventions varied widely, with four studies being part of larger programs involving multiple interventions, while the remaining two were single community mobilization interventions. Both outcomes (skilled birth attendance and facility birth) were reported in three studies, while facility birth alone was reported in the other three studies. All studies reported some benefit of male involvement, either in the presence of a skilled birth attendant (SBA), facility birth, or both. In one before-and-after study, there was a statistically significant increase in the presence of an SBA in the intervention group. Two pre-and-post intervention studies reported a statistically significant increase in facility births for the intervention group, although no data on SBA presence were reported. In a repeat cross-sectional study, women and their husbands reported a statistically significant increase in the use of SBAs and facility births for the exposed group. However, in another repeat cross-sectional study, women reported an increase in SBA presence and facility births for the unexposed group, a finding contradicted by their husbands, who reported an increase in SBA presence and facility births for the exposed group. A program evaluation study found an increased use of facility births in the intervention group. One cluster randomized controlled trial (RCT) of weak methodological quality, and therefore at high risk of bias, reported care with a birth attendant or facility in cases of maternal complications or illness. The participants were women residing in a pre-determined cluster, and the intervention was part of a larger program, making it difficult to isolate the male involvement component. The study reported women visiting hospitals for treatment of problems during pregnancy, with a statistically significant increase in hospital visits for treatment of pregnancy-related problems. Another RCT of weak methodological quality, involving married women attending antenatal care (ANC) with their husbands, reported no significant difference between study groups in the use of more than three ANC visits. The outcome was defined as women attending three or more ANC visits. A cluster RCT of weak methodological quality reported significantly more pregnant women in the intervention arms receiving adequate prenatal care compared to the control arm, but the differences between intervention arms were not significant. For breastfeeding outcomes, one cluster RCT of moderate risk of bias reported breastfeeding at 3–5 and 6-month intervals. The percentage of women commencing mixed feeding was higher in the intervention group than in the control group, but this was not statistically significant. Another study reported significantly more women in the control group continuing exclusive breastfeeding for six months compared to the intervention group. A similar increase was found at three months, but it was not statistically significant. Postpartum care outcomes were also assessed. One RCT of weak methodological quality reported that women assigned to the couples group were significantly more likely to attend a postpartum visit within two weeks of delivery compared to those in the control group or women-alone group. Another study reported no significant difference between men in the control and intervention groups regarding whether their wives had a postpartum check-up. However, a program evaluation study showed an increase in postnatal care within 72 hours of birth post-intervention. Overall, the studies varied greatly in terms of intervention components, populations, and outcomes. Many were part of larger programs, making it difficult to assess the specific impact of male involvement. Most studies were conducted in low-income settings, either rural or urban, and were of weak methodological quality, leading to a high risk of bias. Despite these limitations, some studies reported benefits of male involvement in maternal and newborn health, particularly in increasing facility births, skilled birth attendance, and postpartum care. However, the evidence remains of very low quality due to methodological weaknesses, indirectness, and inconsistency in findings.
